title: Stellar sorting in globular cluster 47 Tucanae
caption: The core of globular cluster 47 Tucanae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 47 Tucanae · constellation Tucana · about 15000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and G. Meylan (École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the crowded core of 47 Tucanae, a globular cluster, a dense ball of stars. Repeated photographs of this region let astronomers follow the 'beehive swarm' motion of its stars, and they measured precise speeds for nearly 15,000 of them.

The work was part of a seven-year study using Hubble. It gave astronomers their strongest observational evidence so far that globular clusters sort their stars by mass. The sorting works like a game of gravitational billiards. As stars pass near one another, heavier stars lose speed and sink toward the core, while lighter stars gain speed and move out toward the edges.

This process is known as mass segregation. Astronomers had long suspected that it happens in globular clusters, but it had never before been directly observed in action. Tracking thousands of individual stars over years finally made that possible.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (0.52 x 0.65 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 2.3 × 2.8 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and repeated sharp Hubble images let astronomers track individual stars in the crowded core.
